html:
Kartini was 20 when she wrote this letter in May 1899 from Jepara, on the north coast of Java in the Dutch East Indies. Her father was the Javanese regent of the town. It was her first letter to Stella Zeehandelaar, a pen friend in the Netherlands. She describes the custom that took noble girls out of school and kept them indoors until marriage.

When I reached the age of twelve, I was kept at home—I must go into the "box." I was locked up, and cut off from all communication with the outside world, toward which I might never turn again save at the side of a bridegroom, a stranger, an unknown man whom my parents would choose for me, and to whom I should be betrothed without my own knowledge. … My parents were inexorable; I went into my prison. Four long years I spent between thick walls, without once seeing the outside world.
How I passed through that time, I do not know. I only know that it was terrible. But there was one great happiness left me: the reading of Dutch books and correspondence with Dutch friends was not forbidden.
I long to be free, to be able to stand alone, to study, not to be subject to any one, and, above all, never, never to be obliged to marry.

She opened a school for girls in 1903 and died in 1904, aged 25, a few days after giving birth.
